newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.S.'s Albright hails peace in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: U.S.'s Albright hails peace in Guatemala.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright praised Guatemala on Sunday for ending its bloody 36-year civil war and said recent peace accords had finally given the strife-torn nation a shot at happiness.

Albright arrived on Sunday for a one-day visit to lend U.S. support to the country's fledgling era of peace after former leftist rebels and the government of Alvaro Arzu signed a peace accord on Dec. 29.

Albright met government officials and their former battlefield adversaries as she toured a guerrilla disarmament camp in northwestern Guatemala, the most visible symbol of peace here after a war that killed at least 100,000 people.

"You have come a long way, and thanks to the peace accords you have a chance to live in peace and happiness," Albright told a crowd of several hundred peasants and former rebels gathered at the camp in Tululche, some 40 miles (65 km) north of Guatemala City.
"These amazing peace accords have provided a blueprint for how Guatemalans ought to live," Albright added.

The makeshift camp was one of eight in Guatemala which housed thousands of former members of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit in the past few months while they turned in their weapons and prepared to return to society after decades of clandestine rebellion.

Albright toured the camp with former rebel Commander Randall, one of the many rebels who were the target of U.S. efforts in the 1970s and 1980s to help the Guatemalan military's anti-insurgency campaign.
Befitting the occasion, Randall dressed in jeans and a t-shirt instead of his old military garb. Albright later handed out colouring books to children from nearby villages.

The event's feel-good atmosphere belied decades of Cold War conflict in the impoverished Central American nation. The United States poured funds into the Guatemalan army during that time, but aid was cut off in 1990 after the U.S. Congress began to look into the army's dismal human rights record.
The United States has promised $40 million a year for the next four years to help Guatemala pay for the costs of implementing the accords.

"We see it as a new and very special sign of the (U.S.) government's interest in the peace process in which they have collaborated," Guatemalan Foreign Minister Stein told reporters shortly before Albright arrived.

Albright was expected to meet President Arzu at his private ranch in southern Guatemala after touring the camp and fly later in the day to Mexico, where President Bill Clinton is due to arrive on Monday.

A centrist businessman, Arzu took power in January, 1996 and by year's end had carried out his campaign pledge to end the civil war. Total pledges of aid for peace from a long list of international donors totals more than $1.9 billion.

Stein said Albright and Arzu would discuss bilateral issues of trade, security and justice, sustainable development and immigration, issues expected to be the central topics at a May 8 summit in Costa Rica between Clinton and his Central American counterparts.
Albright and Stein were also expected to sign an agreement on coordinating efforts to fight car theft.
